The choice of high-quality data for training can greatly enhance the performance of machine learning models. However, when a trained model fails to meet expectations, pinpointing the cause is often an intricate task due to the complex, non-linear nature of modern learning algorithms. This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying the root cause of model issues by integrating the End-to-End (E2E) machine learning framework with Shapley values, resulting in a new metric known as E2E-Shapley. E2E-Shapley evaluates data contributions across various aspects of the E2E learning process, thereby enabling a more comprehensive understanding of why a model is behaving in a certain way.

Radio observations of four nearby Milky Way globular clusters using MAVERIC reveal a previously unknown phenomenon - transient radio bursts originating from the centers of the clusters. These bursts are most intense at 8.56 GHz and decrease at lower and higher frequencies. They are associated with low-luminosity sources, likely in the 10^24 - 10^26 Wb^-1 range. The number of these sources is related to the cluster's stellar stellar count, but the data is currently limited. The duration of these radio bursts is unknown, but they are observed in approximately 10-30% of the observed fields of view, suggesting a minimum duration of days to weeks. The sources are distributed throughout the clusters, with some located near the horizontal branches. They are distinguished from the diffuse radio background by their characteristics - the diffuse background is polarized and concentrated near the cluster cores, whereas the radio bursts are unpolarized and more dispersed. The radio background may result from magnetic dissipation of electrons produced over a longer period, whereas the radio bursts are likely caused by electron destruction in stellar encounters near the end of the cluster's life. Future observations are necessary to determine the sources' lifespans and total production rates.

Recommendation systems based on two graphs have a limited ability to convey information compared to their real-world application scenarios. The existence of additional information beyond edges, such as hyperedges, can be used to convey more context. However, research into recommendation systems based on two graphs does not take into account this extra data. The concept of a triple structure, which combines hypergraphs and two graphs, can be used to represent this context. The proposed hypergraph restoration guidance algorithm retrieves the missing hyperedges by considering this triple structure. A dual objective function is created to balance the recovery of hyperedges and prevention of overfitting. The result is THTRec, a recommendation method based on the triple structure that incorporates learned hyperedges to enhance the model's performance. Comparative studies show that THTRec outperforms existing recommendation methods utilizing multi-information.

Emitting polarized light is crucial for semiconductor devices like lasers and light-emitting diodes. Within these devices, spontaneous photon emission in a specific direction is necessary to generate polarized light. In this work, we utilize an information theory approach to analyze the directional nature of spontaneous discharges in a microcavity laser structure capable of emitting in two distinct directions. By applying entropy calculations, our study reveals that the most probable configuration corresponds to a state with a notable difference in photon discharges, which is distinct from a symmetric 50/50 distribution. This work demonstrates the utility of entropy as a tool for analyzing systems with spontaneous behavior, which can only occur in a non-symmetric way.

The precise measurement of spin and temperature in warm alkali metal clouds is crucial for the successful execution of alkali metal collective quantum processes like superfluidity. A method introduced and methodically validated in this study extracts thermal and spin information from a warm alkali metal cloud by analyzing photon emission spectra. The line shapes of these spectra are directly linked to the cloud's temperature and spin distribution, respectively. Furthermore, the imaging technique demonstrated in this research can be optimized to minimize errors in the inferred parameters. Another significant finding is the observation of spontaneous spin fluctuations in a group of thermal rubidium atoms, reminiscent of the Moessbauer effect but occurring in a spontaneously manner in a warm, dense atomic ensemble.

Most existing research on offline reinforcement learning for multiple interacting agents relies on labeled interaction outcomes, such as those used in joint training methods. In contrast, there is relatively little work examining how individual agents can be trained independently. We investigate the potential for single-agent offline reinforcement learning in interactions and show that it can still achieve satisfactory performance. We also propose an offline learning approach for agents that learn from any agent in a positive trajectory. We propose two methods for offline education: one where the learner is limited to an observed trajectory and another where the learner can execute additional interactions. We assess our approach in an eight-player StarCraft II game and confirm that it can lead to positive outcomes. We also compare it to state-of-the-art single-agent offline methods and agents trained on data from the interaction.

Converting MV images into CT images is known as 2D/3D image registration, a crucial step before delivering MV images for patient treatment in radiotherapy. Traditional methods of using image intensifiers or flat panel detectors in MV imaging are being replaced by on-board MV imaging, making 2D/3D registration necessary. Due to the low image quality and differences in how images are acquired, this conversion can be a challenging task. Traditional methods of alignment are often inefficient and produce inaccurate results, prompting researchers to explore the use of deep learning techniques for a more effective solution. A new approach using a convolutional neural network has been developed for aligning MV and CT images, with various network designs being tested for their effectiveness. Using a dataset of 120 patients, the best performing algorithm was found to yield alignment errors of less than a millimeter when used in radiotherapy treatments, demonstrating the potential for deep learning methods to excel in 2D/3D image registration.

Researchers often use local operations and classical communication (LOCC) to verify quantum correlations between distant parties. To our knowledge, the method involves verifying the output state after applying a quantum operation to an initial state. We challenge this approach when dealing with scenarios where the initial state exists in separate locations but becomes inaccessible. We argue that in cases where the state is represented as a superposition of distinct, spatially separated particles, nonlocal effects can arise solely from an local quantum operation applied to one particle. To our knowledge, these effects can mimic the nonlocal guidance experienced by the other particle.

As autonomous vehicles become increasingly prevalent, they offer numerous benefits but also present significant security concerns. To address this, researchers are proposing the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), which brings both opportunities and risks. A secure and dependable IoV system requires robust privacy protection measures. In this paper, a comprehensive review of research on privacy protection for blockchain-enabled federated education frameworks in IoV is presented. By examining existing studies, the following characteristics of these frameworks are identified: suitable blockchain technologies, effective access control methods, and reliable privacy protection techniques such as homomorphic encryption and secure channel communications. Additionally, the limitations of current proposals are identified, and a set of evaluation criteria are established to assess their performance. This research paves the way for the development of a secure and private blockchain-enabled federated education framework for IoV in the near future.

V392 Persei, a classical nova that erupted in 2018, is notable for being one of the rare visible novae observed since its discovery in March of 2018. By combining data from various observatories, researchers have determined the characteristics of V392 Pe, which is currently in a transitional phase between its nova outburst and white dwarf remnant phases. V392 Pe's nova outburst emitted a significant amount of gamma-ray luminosity, which was on par with other high-energy gamma-ray novae. Observations suggest that the system is undergoing a reverse shock, which is occurring within a dense wind ejected during the nova outburst. By comparing the properties of V392 Pe to other gamma-ray luminous novae, scientists have been able to develop a radiative transfer model that simulates the system's behavior during its outburst. V392 Pe's estimated binary period is around 10.8 days, and the system is expected to recapture its companion in a few hundred years.

To maintain error correction, the toric code necessitates operations on adjacent qubits. 
However, faulty memory modules can execute successful but unintended multi-qubit operations, 
known as logical operations, that happen when planned separate single-qubit operations 
coincidentally occur at the same time. 
These unintentional logical operations can't be handled by the standard 2D syndrome 
measurement process, rendering it incapable of identifying and rectifying the resulting 
errors. 
To address this issue, we present a method to contain these unintentional multi-qubit 
operations inside the topological framework, and demonstrate that, when such 
unintended logical operations are limited to those affecting three or fewer qubits, 
the standard 2D measurement process can be modified to identify and correct them, 
reducing the overhead for error correction in comparison to the errors that happen 
during unsuccessful Planar Gate operations. 
This finding highlights the significant error-correction advantages of executing 
planned simultaneous two-qubit operations on participating qubits.

For resolving severe uplink/downlink asymmetry in modern wireless networks,
long-term uplink statistics knowledge at the base station is crucial.  Leveraging
these statistics, the base station can optimize downlink precoding in a
two-step process: first, it develops an expanded codebook based on Gaussean
mixture models from uplink data, and then selects a smaller final codebook by
encoding the GMM parameters shared between the base station and mobile device.
This paper presents a novel scheme for codebook development and selection that
leverages the uplink data and GMM parameters encoding, addressing the lack of
channel state information at the mobile station. We evaluate various methods for
encoding the GMM parameters, considering both real-world and simulated FDD
scenarios and various codebook sizes. Our results indicate that a certain
codebook size yields the highest data rate in both types of FDD scenarios. We
also show the impact of the number of GMM components and the encoding method
on the achieved data rate.

We analyze the boundary behavior of two-dimensional fermions confined within a metal cavity that exhibits the 2D Hofstadter spectrum. A robust form of chiral diffusion is found at the cavity's edges, characterized by its insensitivity to lattice structure and stability across various nonequilibrium states. This type of current distribution can be understood through the concept of chiral tomography. Our findings indicate that nonequilibrium chiral surface currents maintain their behavior, unaffected by the degree of nonequilibrium. This is in contrast to conventional Hall currents, which can turn back under high levels of nonequilibrium. Our study provides a theoretical basis for experiments using semiconducting or semiconductor heterostructures, as well as cold atomic systems, to observe chiral surface tomography in detail.

Bondi mass shedding by black holes in the center of active galactic nuclei has been theoretically explored, but currently, there is a lack of empirical data to inform models due to the difficulty of detecting active black holes at the minimum accretion levels. It is argued that the minimum mass growth rate for supermassive black holes should be at least related to the Bondi mass shedding rate, which will have an impact on the initial conditions for Population III star formation. Although the minimum mass growth rate could be as high as 10^-3 times the Bondi rate based on theoretical considerations, more recent findings suggest that relativistic outflows may significantly reduce this limit to several orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, it is shown that a more precise minimum mass growth rate can be directly derived from the Bondi formula, which should be at least 10^-10 times the Bondi rate, corresponding to a minimum supermassive black hole mass of approximately 10^4 solar masses for a given set of surrounding gas properties.

We investigate the potential of detecting low-frequency gravitational waves using pulsar timing arrays, specifically from merging supermassive black holes in dense clusters of stars around galaxies. Previous studies have focused on dense populations of stellar-mass black holes, but the potential of merging large mass black holes in the centers of these star clusters has been largely overlooked. Although a significant fraction of large mass black holes may reside in wide binaries or unbound orbits, the Three Body Relaxed distribution predicts that nearly all of them will settle into the cores of these clusters following gravitational interactions. Moreover, three-body interactions are expected to frequently produce black holes in extremely dense, close orbits that could generate detectable gravitational waves signals in pulsar timing arrays. This scenario would be consistent with observations of the magnetic fields of some galaxies, which often exhibit a power-law distribution.

Gamma-Ray Bursts are enigmatic high-energy phenomena that originate in the deep universe, often signaling the end of massive stars' lives or the type Ia supernovae. To accurately interpret data from China's Gravitational Wave high-Energy Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, a precise BR Simulator is crucial for detecting Gamma-Ray Bursts. This study assesses a compact Gamma-Ray Burst Simulator built on a mobile device, adhering to the GECAM's detection criteria. The new simulator's accuracy is tested against the GECAM's BR Scanner, with results showing comparable true positive and false positive rates, indicating its capability to faithfully replicate Gamma-Ray Burst signals.

This paper extends the study of Semigroups of Composing Tensors and Customized Operators within BMOA-like spaces to a more general setting, specifically 'BMOA-like' spaces. First, we generalize the definition of the original space $\mathcal{B}_\omega$ to a broader class of spaces $\mathcal{B}_\omega$, and then characterize its associated BMOA space. Additionally, we analyze the conditions under which the Semigroup of Composing Tensors and the Integral Operators are bounded within the $\mathcal{B}_\omega$ and $\mathcal{B}\mathcal{M}\mathcal{O}\mathcal{A}_\omega$ spaces.

It is widely assumed that an increase in scientific output signifies greater knowledge, yet this assumption is questionable. This question arises from the observed disparity between the highly prolific authors and the vast majority of researchers who publish with lower frequency. Using unique ID numbers from established databases such as DBpedia and Wikidata, we directly measured the average number of facts conveyed in the references of articles from the computer science field. Our study's results indicate that adding a paper to a research group's work does not necessarily increase knowledge. Furthermore, research giants do not possess greater knowledge than their lesser-known counterparts. These findings suggest a nuanced understanding of the relationship between knowledge and scientific publication, which currently lacks a clear model.

In a multi-carrier wireless communication system with an amplifying relay, we investigate the physical layer security between a source transmitter and an intended recipient, while preventing eavesdroppers from intercepting the message. By analyzing the situation where both channels to the recipient and to the eavesdropper are composed of disjoint sub-channels, an optimal strategy for allocating power and assigning sub-channels to the direct and relayed paths is determined. Furthermore, a useful bound for the secure capacity under general channels is established, characterized by an increase due to the relay. This bound aids in evaluating the performance of various physical layer protocols, including an allocation method for power and sub-channels that benefits the communication. Our results show the secure capacity in a practical scenario, obtained through a combination of physical layer protocols, to be close to this bound, indicating a significant improvement achieved by these methods.

Two-dimensional systems with edge transport and localized quantum anomalies are useful in various applications, especially for engineering two-dimensional qubits that interact with a multi-channel waveguide. By utilizing a tight-binding model, we have demonstrated that a central defect can effectively mediate long-range interactions between channels through a two-dimensional ferromagnet. This leads to the formation of hybrid states that combine edge modes at different locations, offering robust protection against non-unitary noise. Additionally, controlling the topological properties of the system allows us to switch between two distinct types of edge modes. This switching ability can be utilized to create quantum logic gates between qubits. Furthermore, we have explored the possibility of creating entangled states using Jaynes-Cummings ladders, as well as realizing state swap operations and Bell states through the coupling of adjacent sites.

This study explores the application of predictive technology in managing automated vehicles at a single traffic signal junction. Using a novel method that combines machine learning with real-time data, we infer optimal speed and journey planning for each vehicle. A traffic signal timing system based on predictive information is proposed to enhance overall traffic flow and safety. We assess the effectiveness of our approach through a comprehensive simulation of one junction, which includes data from actual vehicles and a data-driven prediction model. The results show that our method can significantly enhance both safety and efficiency, demonstrating its potential for practical implementation.

Text-based games provide a complex environment for AI to practice solving,
with the risk of solving them paving the way for AI to understand real-world
situations more effectively. To better train its programs, NLP relies on
realistic text-based scenarios. However, efficiently simulating these games
at a high speed is challenging due to the time-consuming nature of calculating
actual game elements. We addressed this issue by creating an incredibly fast
game simulator called TextWorldExpress, enabling significantly faster calculation
of any given state's score and potentially benefiting other promising approaches
like Monte Carlo Tree Search.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on recurrent neural networks, have gained significant popularity in various applications involving video analysis.  However, training and running these models have proven to be computationally expensive and time-consuming.  As an answer, we propose a novel solution that combines algorithmic and hardware advancements to develop highly energy-efficient deep learning models for video understanding.  Our algorithmic-hardware co-design strategy focuses on identifying objects from videos using long short-term memory networks, and we introduce a new method called hierarchical tucker tensor decomposition for parallel processing and tensor factorization on tensor processing units.  This new technique is expected to reduce data size, enable parallel computation, and lead to a more compact and precise deep learning model.  We also designed a custom tensor processing unit to accelerate the training and execution of these models, and our evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements in terms of runtime, model size, and accuracy compared to conventional approaches.

Restricted Data Learning in NLP occurs when pre-trained language models are fine-tuned on a target task with fewer GPU memory available than model size. This phenomenon limits model capacity and hinders the acquisition of crucial information. We conducted an experimental analysis to identify which specific information is most important for a model to learn during a typical fine-tuning process. Building on this, we proposed a new enhancement strategy to provide models with additional pseudo information, allowing them to process more comprehensive data within their limited memory. Our experiments show that two proposed information enhancement methods can achieve performance comparable to standard fine-tuning using an unfathomably larger model. Moreover, we developed a quantifiable metric to evaluate the model's information processing capability and developed a theoretical framework to guide future design of information enhancement strategies.

The idea of charged elements being convex in certain algebras, first proposed by Connes and Dyson, has significant implications for the study of CFTs in d dimensions. By applying this concept to the algebra of operators in a regularized d-dimensional CFT, the convexity of charged elements implies the feeble gravity conjecture, which predicts the appearance of black holes with arbitrarily low masses as we increase the regularization scale beyond d=3. The convexity of charged elements is demonstrated for the algebras associated with regularized 2-dimensional CFTs, providing support for the conjecture that the feeble gravity conjecture and the T-duality of CFTs are mutually reinforcing.

To tackle complex systems in quantum field theory and many-body physics, we need to balance computational efficiency with physical accuracy. Methods using quantum imaginary duration evolution in a balanced framework are an effective solution, involving the refinement of computational models through imaginary time averaging. Introducing a model-space quantum imaginary duration balanced procedure, we can achieve this balance by introducing a new operator that enables the optimization of model parameters, leading to enhanced stability and accuracy, and potential application to systems that are difficult to simulate due to fermion sign problems.

We introduce a new concept called the compact Hilbert polynomial, specifically for power series rings that possess finite characteristic and apply to excellent local rings of higher dimensions with positive regular primes. This new definition enables us to prove that local rings with the property of being F-pure or having F-singularities are deeply embedded, which had previously only been established for one-dimensional rings. This result also provides a new, more straightforward proof of a theorem by Hochster and Huneke regarding the deep embedding of regular local rings.

This study suggests a new approach to procuring support services in the renewable energy sector by analyzing how market involvement affect project success. Investigating the issue from this perspective is unique in the current literature. Research was conducted using 111 case studies from the UK's onshore wind and solar photovoltaic markets. Case selection aimed to provide a representative sample of market experiences. The study found that a range of support services are needed for both technology and experience-lacking projects and that they impact project effectiveness. The influence of market involvement on project success is also identified. The research leads to a set of recommendations for providing targeted support based on market involvement, and the need for further investigation in other sectors and countries. The study's findings have the potential to guide policy decisions in the energy and other infrastructure sectors reliant on new technologies.

Given complex polynomials $P$ and $Q$ with degrees $d_P$ and $d_Q$, denoted as $d$, we define the 'prime focus set' of $P_z: z \mapsto P(z^2)$ and 'iterates of the combined polynomials' focus set" of $P_z$ and $Q_z$, where $P_z(z) = P(z^2)$ and $Q_z(z) = Q(z^2)$. 

Building on previous work by the author and D. Schleicher, this paper extends the concepts and findings related to the prime focus set and iterates of the combined polynomials focus set from quadratic polynomials to higher-degree complex polynomials of degree $d > 2$. 

This research is inspired by the observation that quadratic maps $z \mapsto z^2$ behave similarly to higher-degree maps in certain aspects, specifically near infinity, as noted in reference [10].

This study investigates Higgs boson pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, with a focus on a specific decay channel involving bottom quarks and $WW$ pairs. To tackle computational challenges associated with the complex final state, the research employs the matrix element method to tackle the distinct dynamics of bottom quark generation and Higgs boson decay, thereby enabling more efficient phase space sampling and reducing Monte Carlo uncertainties. As a result, it is possible to achieve a four-times improvement in statistical uncertainty, which in turn enables a more precise LHC cross-section prediction in this particular channel.

We use a theoretical framework consisting of two Higgs doublets and an singlet scalar to determine the effects on the standard process of the $e^+e^-\to Zh$ reaction and the standard deviation sigma of the Higgs boson decay to two photons. 

Our analysis covers the standard case where one of the scalars in our model decays to a pair of photons via a loop, which corresponds to measuring the cross section of the aforementioned reaction as a function of the center of mass energy. 

We also investigate the expanded scalar sector in the case where the two photons have an invariant mass distribution, which is relevant for future linear colliders. 

In order to constrain the model parameters, we consider outcomes from the linear collider up to 500 GeV, which is based on projections from the ILC.

Recent observations from the Saturnian polar region have revealed the presence of a high-latitude, cool gas loop that has started to form a closed loop, or polar vortex, just before the summer solstice.  If this vortex holds until the equinox, it would be a groundbreaking event, as no such prolonged survival has ever been observed before.  In anticipation of this development, our team has created a high-resolution, global atmospheric model that has already successfully replicated various features of Saturn's atmosphere.  In order to simulate the unexpected survival of this vortex, we have incorporated an additional atmospheric loop in the model.  Interestingly, this loop generates localized barotropic and baroclinic wave disturbances that disrupt the deformation of the equator-to-pole flow, allowing the vortex to persist.  As an alternative solution, our team has also discovered a specific atmospheric hexagon shape located near the pole, slightly offset from the spin axis, that can maintain this vortex through axisymmetric deformation.  If observed, this hexagon could provide valuable insights into the formation of Saturn's famous hexagon at Saturn's north pole.

For a convex obstacle in two or more dimensions, we're analyzing a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with an infinite potential barrier, focusing on solutions that disappear at a finite time. It's proven that under certain conditions, these solutions always vanish completely at their time of extinction, regardless of the nature of the boundary. Additionally, an upper bound is established for the time of extinction, involving a specific geometric property of the convex obstacle. This bound can also be applied to a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation modeling a trap with a finite diameter, providing an upper limit for the time of extinction in that scenario as well.

We present a novel semi-parametric local-charset approximation method for polynomial equations, enabling the transformation of a variety's description into a set of equations that include the equation's coefficients from $\mathbb{Q}$, and this local-charset formulation is consistent across all possible characteristic types, including zero, and we demonstrate the method's effectiveness by formulating the equations for the Deligne-Irving modular curve and recovering the Deligne-Irving modular curve when the characteristic is zero.

The transition behavior of V$_2$O$_3$ thin films is influenced by their thickness, with some studies indicating a metal-to-insulator transition shift as the thickness decreases.  However, previous experiments on V$_2$O$_3$ have yielded inconclusive findings due to varying results.  Using in-situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we investigated the properties of V$_2$O$_3$ films deposited on Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) substrates and observed a metal-to-insulator transition shift as the thickness decreased below 5.6 nm.  This metal-to-insulator transition shift is attributed to surface oxidation induced by oxygen exposure, as evidenced by temperature-dependent measurements performed in a vacuum.  Additionally, theoretical calculations suggest that oxygen exposure can alter the crystal structure of V$_2$O$_3$, which in turn affects its electronic properties.  Our study highlights the critical role of surface modification in determining the metal-to-insulator transition behavior of V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films.

Our study uncovers the precise long-distance behavior of one-dimensional mixtures of two bosonic species subject to attractive interactions, demonstrating the presence of quantum effects. By employing finite-size scaling analysis of type-A and type-C singularities in different system sizes and boundary conditions, we directly measure quantum scale lan$\delta$ and quantum phase stiffness $\Theta$ for various systems. The relationship $\Theta \propto \hbar^2/(2m)\cdot 1/\delta$ is verified, providing a method to manipulate quantum phase stiffness for stable quantum state transfer. Additionally, a quantum simulation of dynamics of a double dark-soliton is achieved using a dual BEC system, demonstrating the feasibility of utilizing such structures as multi-particle barriers for coherent state transfer.

We introduce the concept of polarization for homogeneous collections of vector fields defined on arbitrary manifolds, and demonstrate that a polarized collection of graded fields can be uniquely transformed into its corresponding homogenous collection.

Let $G$ be a quasi-split group of the same type over a field of positive characteristic $p$. If $p$ is greater than the Coxeter number of $G$, we demonstrate that the standardization of a measure on $G$ can be achieved by integrating the product of quasi-characters over a set representing each un conjugacy class. This result is then applied to identify the factor standardizing the orbital measure for specific elements within $G$.

Recent advancements in high-brilliance x-ray sources have enabled the use of non-resonant and synchrotron x-ray scattering in studying the unique properties of Cu-pyrochlore chlorides, which break time-reversal symmetry. In these materials, a peculiar state known as the magnetic pyrochlore nuclear phase has been discovered. In this phase, the electron spins are anti-parallel to the nuclear spins in a pyrochlore structure, making resonant x-ray scattering a highly effective technique for detecting this extremely weak scattering phenomenon. Using non-polarized synchrotron x-ray scattering, researchers were able to measure the exchange-charged correlations that underlie the magnetic pyrochlore nuclear phase. In addition, using a high-brilliance x-ray beamline, researchers were able to observe short-range exchange-charged correlations that may be a key component for the formation of this exotic state of matter.

Quantum error correction is an indispensable component for building functional quantum computers, yet determining optimal thresholds for various quantum codes and circuit designs has been a challenging task. This study introduces a novel approach, based on an adapted Potts model, to analyze the error correction capabilities of both code families and specific circuit configurations. This method enables precise calculation of threshold errors, through simulations of Monte Carlo, in moderately time-consuming tasks. We apply this approach to analyze the surface code, its hybrid variants, and a quantum code based on twisted XZ codes, as well as quantum parity check circuits susceptible to biased errors. Our results reveal that the proposed spin model can accurately predict quantum thresholds, often matching Monte Carlo outcomes within a narrow margin. This framework is versatile and can assess any code or circuit configuration, facilitating more efficient parameter calculations. Notably, our analysis of the surface code with two-qubit biased errors and quantum parity checks with faulty circuits yields new essential threshold findings.

Recent theoretical predictions have highlighted the outstanding properties of a new 2D material, tellurene, in H. Wang et al.'s research. With 4 stable configurations available, especially the fully relaxed low-energy state, tellurene displays exceptional characteristics. Its fully open energy gap, up to 1.14 eV, combined with rich band topology, including large and negative values of the 2D spin Hall conductivity, make it stand out among 2D materials. Moreover, its controllable 2D spin conductivity can be altered through strain, while its topological characteristics remain intact. Moreover, advanced calculations have indicated that functionalization with hydrogen, fluorine, chlorine, hydroxyl, and methyl groups maintains large spin Hall conductance values. These findings suggest that the unique properties of tellurene can be preserved even after modification, making it a promising candidate for 2D topological applications.

This study examines single-phase Darcy flow through fractured rock formations. A new numerical approach is introduced, combining the finite element and boundary element methods to model flow in matrix blocks and fractures respectively. The discrete displacement model is decoupled from the flow simulation, which is efficiently handled using the hybrid-combined finite element technique. Several solvers are compared in a test case to evaluate their convergence properties, with results indicating that the HC0 element offers the optimal balance of computational cost and solution accuracy.

To create compact spin-switches, a solitary spiral magnetic layer with uniform spiral orientation is suggested, offering energy efficiency and quick switching speeds.  A current passing through the spiral layer causes the spin-polarized current-MEE effect, which modifies the spiral's magnetization state and subsequently alters the resistance in an adjacent normal metal layer.  A key benefit of this design is its reliance solely on the first harmonic of the spiral's resistance, which is controlled by the up-down magnetization of the outer rim of the spiral, allowing for a more effective and streamlined switching process.  A practical demonstration of this concept was carried out using a Pt/Co/MgO device featuring a 4-nm cobalt spiral layer, where the spin resistance change was observed to be 0.44 Ω, corresponding to about 0.6 kΩ in terms of sheet resistance.

A Bayes factor stands out as a key element in Bayesian inference using subjective priors, yet it poses significant difficulties in establishing objective priors. To overcome this challenge, we introduce the concept of Bayesian confirmatory inference and present eight methods to employ Bayes factors effectively. These methods are then applied to two diverse scenarios: assessing the effectiveness of a new medication in a medical clinical trial and the success of a new technology in a clinical clinical trial.

Discourse markers that signify connections between sentences can be misinterpreted by current AI systems, as their meaning depends on individual contexts. To enhance the robustness of discourse annotation, our study proposes DiscSense, a contextual approach that uses machine learning to identify potentially meaningful discussions between sentences. By reducing the number of sentences to review and accurately detecting meaningful discourse cases, our model's discourses were verified as having verified contextual meaning by human evaluators.

Quantum information processing utilizing optical resonance of the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond is hindered by temperature-related errors. To address this, a set of microwave and laser frequencies is required to maintain the system's ground state, and an elevated temperature is simulated. As a result, the spectral characteristics are significantly altered at higher temperatures, and, in addition, multiple ground state configurations are identified at 500K and 600K through detailed analysis.

The brains of higher mammals process information in specialized areas and refines that information in a complex network of interconnected cortical regions. A key puzzle in neuroscience research is to comprehend how the brain's distinct functional regions and complex interconnections emerge and develop. Studies have shown that local groups of neural cells can act like simple neural networks that make decisions and process information, which in turn influences the more comprehensive interregional network. This research suggests that a more comprehensive model, which includes these locally informative neural cells and their relationship with the broader network, may provide valuable insights into how the brain processes information. By creating a simulated model that includes these elements, researchers can start to unravel the complex dynamics of information in the brain.

Investigating the long-range spin correlations in an SU(3) AFM system on a triangular lattice, a crucial aspect of triangular-based Bravais lattices, required adjusting the Heisenberg model with two additional parameters, namely sextuplet and octuplet AFM interactions, and simulating various exchange couplings using path integral and exact diagonalization techniques. Two distinct phases, characterized by distinct wavefunction patterns, were identified in this study: first, a spin liquid state on the triangular sublattice, and second, a zigzag spin density wave state on a zigzag path. The transition to these phases occurs abruptly, with residual entropy values of 0.18 and 0.23, respectively. Furthermore, examination of spin-LRO in this system showed that it arises from the spin-1 component in both identified phases. A mapping of this Heisenberg model to an $SU(3)$ SUFE model yielded a localized moment value of 1 for the spin-1 state, with implications for describing the magnetic properties of QCD mesons.

A novel implementation of the Hartree-Fock-Rock method for atomic systems in arbitrary central fields has been devised, based on a flexible B-spline framework for system geometry and electron interactions. This versatile approach enables efficient and accurate calculations suitable for comparing multiple scenarios in a direct manner, whether in atoms, clusters, or fluid systems. The method was demonstrated to be highly accurate for a wide range of atomic cases, including low-lying states in various atoms with central fields, and also yielded precise results for an electron system confined within a 3D spherical boundary. The obtained total energies and radial distributions matched closely with existing high-accuracy benchmarks, and the method's efficiency was further highlighted by the relatively brief computation time. The B-spline framework's adaptability and ease of implementation were also showcased, and the associated BFORKS computer code is available for further exploration.

The study of time-crystals has recently given rise to universal standard time signals that exhibit explosive synchronization, a phenomenon where oscillators suddenly synchronize in response to weakening coupling. Although previous research into explosive synchronization has been confined to coupled pendulums, this study aims to investigate the conditions of this phenomenon using a different system of coupled torsion balances that exhibit explosive synchronization at the point of decoupling. By experimentally exploring various types of oscillators, frequencies, and environments, this study establishes a new standard for explosive synchronization that can be utilized to better understand and predict its behavior in different systems.

Fixed-rank matrix optimization problems are prevalent in numerous applications and are often non-convex from a Euclidean perspective. However, from a Riemannian perspective, some of these problems exhibit convex or geodesically convex properties on subspaces. This paper delves into the analysis of optimization landscapes from a worldwide perspective, considering both Euclidean and Riemannian viewpoints. We explore the relationships between critical points and submanifolds and propose efficient algorithms to find optimal solutions on these landscapes. Notably, some previously studied optimization problems with complex landscapes are found to be geodesically convex from a Riemannian perspective. We provide proof of this property and analyze the impact of adding convex regularizers. Furthermore, we provide proof of the existence of optimal solutions for fixed-rank positive semi-definite matrix factorization and weighted image reconstruction.

In recent research on the robust edge-disjoint cubic bipartite graphs problem, bipartite graphs with a large number of edges are being examined. A study from four years ago by three researchers demonstrated that most such graphs are capable of being colored with three edge-disjoint cubic bipartite graphs, but the definition of 'almost all' was not clearly established. In this article, the work of those researchers is continued with the creation of a counterexample consisting of four edge-disjoint cubic bipartite graphs within the set of all edge pairs of a particular bipartite graph, yet when two of those graphs are removed, the remaining graph is not able to be decomposed into two edge-disjoint cubic bipartite graphs. This counterexample is also shown to hold true for sufficiently large'n'.

Let $L(\chi,d)$ denote the Dirichlet character $L$-function. This paper delves into specific identities associated with gamma factors within the functional equation of $L(\chi,s)$, where $\chi$ is either a primitive Dirichlet character or not.

A novel, unstable particle concept is put forth, which could have mass up to an EeV scale and extremely low abundance in the universe, derived from new physics beyond the Standard Model. These particles, which have 'long' interaction paths, might be tied to the formation of structure during the universe's expansion, such as primordial black holes or the early universe's inflation. A new theoretical framework is developed, introducing the 'cosmic thread abundance parameter' to describe the density of these particles based on their concentration around massive objects. We then explore the properties of two types of particles, the 'stable' and 'quasistable' kinds, which decay either instantly or after a finite distance, 'long lifetimes,' through one of the Standard Model processes, such as beta decay. A model is also created, which shows how these particles could resolve the 'Fermi-LAT 511 keV anomaly', if they were produced around massive objects, such as neutron stars, and before the universe's recombination era.

The study investigates how the properties of the surrounding fluid, specifically its zero-shear viscoelasticity, affect the swimming speed and pattern of a viscoelastic fluid by a helically coiled swimmer made of two different materials. It is found that viscoelastic forces can cause the swimming path to shift from smooth to oscillatory. When the swimmer is uniformly made of one material, increasing viscoelastic forces can lead to a decrease in swimming speed. Conversely, a vissoelastically made swimmer with a front part rigid and rear viscoelastic can experience an enhancement in swimming speed. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a specific ratio of the viscoelastic and rigid parts can result in optimal swimming performance.

In this research, we applied evolutionary and cooperative game theory concepts to develop a method for reaching a Nash equilibrium in a two-player symmetric Cournot game. Specifically, we utilized a modified, coevolutionary genetic algorithm to simultaneously update the strategies of the players and their respective payoff functions. It was demonstrated that this approach converges to a Nash equilibrium, offering an effective method for implementing the Nash equilibrium concept in practice. Furthermore, a single run of the algorithm produces a profile of strategies at the Nash equilibrium, which can be employed in the laboratory to replicate the outcomes of the experiment and analyze players' behavior.

As the size of Ontologies continues to expand, maintaining their conceptual clarity and coherence becomes increasingly difficult, especially given their limited ability to adapt to new information, especially when structured freely. Leveraging the ability to extract insights from unorganized data, we propose a method to identify hidden concepts within text and suggest adding them to an Ontology, supplementing traditional knowledge acquisition models that rely on structured data. We also introduce a novel approach to mapping relationships between identified concepts and concepts in the Ontology, using a series of classifiers. Experimental results show that our method works effectively with Labeled Corpora, while efficiency is improved by utilizing pre-trained language models and parallel processing.

A novel approach has been devised to model nonequilibrium steady states using an Ising-doped elector population on a complete graph, representing a system isolated from its surroundings. A two-tiered framework is created where a complete graph of spin-based 'dopants' exerts an influence on a larger population of mean-field Ising electrons. It has been found that a particular level of external input can induce a steady state that closely resembles an equilibrium thermodynamic state, and at this point, the system's conduct conductivity can be calculated. Furthermore, an analytical derivation has been performed for the conduct on the boundary of input levels, and a numerical simulation has been conducted for the entire framework, revealing that an insulator-to-conductor transition occurs in a distinct two-step process.

This research examines how viruses transmitted through aerosols propagate under different environmental conditions. A computational model is used to analyze changes in viral concentration in the air and on surfaces, taking into account temperature and humidity variations. The study finds that higher temperatures and low humidity generally favor the survival of aerosol-transmitted viruses, whereas moderate humidity may be more beneficial for surface-borne viruses. The model is applied to understand SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS outbreaks and their patterns of transmission. Additionally, the concept of weather-facilitated viruses is introduced, which refers to viruses whose spread is influenced by environmental conditions, in contrast to climate-sensitive viruses.

Ambiguity represents a primary obstacle to scientific machine intelligence systems accurately replicating human problem-solving capabilities. Currently, there is a lack of unified methods for evaluating the reliability of machine intelligence information and recommendations. This paper provides an overview of various ambiguity measurement approaches used in scientific machine learning, along with relevant assessment strategies. We discuss the limitations of current methods and suggest avenues for enhancing them, with a focus on the role of confidence in preventing overconfident but inaccurate machine learning outputs.
Given a weighted directed graph, we've identified the common and symbolic powers of the edge ideal's ring in relation to its directed edge ideal.

Using the exact density of states for the anti-fundamental matrix, a specific non-critical type $B$ matrix model at a finite $N$ is developed.
This development leads to a formulation of an effective potential in a large $N$ limit for a matrix model where both an $N\times N$ and an $(N+1)\times (N+1)$ matrix are considered, assuming a large $N$ limit where the $(N+1)\times (N+1)$ matrix size scales as $O(N)$.
The effective potential is found to be analogous to the vacuum V-shells in an $N$-body quantum problem for a complex matrix.
The large $N$ effective potential displays two distinct phases, corresponding to various V-shell configurations.
These phases are linked to the penetration of an additional sphere in an $N$-body system into a confined space.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are frequently deployed in safety-critical systems, where ensuring robustness against malfunctions is of paramount importance. Despite advances in design techniques and manufacturing processes, semiconductor chips are prone to failures caused by heat, moisture, and physical impacts. Although researchers commonly assess the accuracy and efficiency of CNNs using standard metrics, they neglect to consider the impact of failures on the performance and safety of these models. To address this gap, we introduce a new framework for analyzing the resilience of hardware in CNNs, called HWR-CNN. This framework enables a comprehensive evaluation of the robustness of CNNs to potential malfunctions at the individual neuron level. Building on this, we introduce a design strategy, HWR-CNN, that incorporates activation range monitoring to create more reliable and secure hardware for CNNs.

The challenge of calculating financial obligations within enterprises can be effectively addressed using a Petri net-based approach, which offers simplicity, clarity, and a universal language for modeling processes across various domains. In this study, we demonstrate how to utilize this net structure to calculate the amounts due between companies according to Romanian Ministry of Finance regulations. Specifically, we focus on determining debt balances based on remittance data, such as invoices and payment receipts, to be used in financial reconciliation processes known as the "compensation of claims" procedure. The algorithm used in this study has been successfully implemented within the Romanian Ministry of Finance's system for automating this process.

Researchers have explored various twist modifications in the Jordanian $r$-matrix, resulting in multiple twist versions. By applying a specific technique to adjust the matrix without altering its properties, a broader family of Jordanian twists has been identified. This study applies the Jordanian twist to the Longhi-Diodi Hamiltonian and another quadratic Hamiltonian, yielding equivalent forms. The process has been generalized for any 2-tori deformed harmonic oscillators and their quadratic Hamiltonians.

We propose a shared semantic framework that enables rapid and automatic knowledge acquisition from numerous languages, resulting in a language-agnostic word vector space. By ensuring cluster consistency across different linguistic sources using a self-supervised technique, we introduce a word representation method. This approach involves a series of word2vec training on individual language datasets and refinement through a consistency loss, ultimately producing a unified, multi-lingual word representation. The proposed method is evaluated on eleven languages and the results demonstrate its superiority over prominent alternatives in both clustering and downstream tasks.

This analysis identifies and characterizes pions, kaons, protons, anti-protons, phi mesons produced in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV. Data collected with the CMS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider form the basis of this study. We describe pion production through a combination of direct measurement and phi meson reconstruction, while kaon analysis focuses on protonting, given limited direct detection. For Xe-Xe collisions, we calculate normalized differential cross-sections for various hadron types across multiple final-state momenta and rapidities, comparing the results to lead-lead collision data and various theoretical models. Additionally, we estimate relative contribution of various sources to final-state hadrons based on the p/T ratio and find pion production dominated by direct pion source at high momentum in both collisions types, whereas in lead-lead collisions, a recombination model aligns well with observed hadron spectra, in contrast to xenon-xenon collisions.

We've identified the primary issue with low-quality annotated data for conversation state tracking (CST) as label noise, which significantly hampers performance due to the manual annotation process. Despite numerous state-of-the-art models and techniques being developed, they fail to effectively address the noise issue. In response, we've created the first noise-aware CST framework, called ASSIST, which integrates an attention mechanism and a start-time signal to produce two distinct CST outputs, thereby allowing for the selection of the most reliable annotation during training. We've conducted comprehensive experiments on various public datasets, where ASSIST has consistently outperformed various models in terms of both exact and weighted F-scores, demonstrating its superior capability in handling the label noise issue.

In late October 2019, large-scale demonstrations in Chile's major cities turned violently anti-government. These events stemmed from the assassination of former police chief Manuel Abreu, but quickly acquired a broader socio-political context. Abreu's killer was apprehended within hours, yet the protests persisted for weeks. To better understand the underlying causes of this prolonged unrest, a new mathematical model is required. The existing Abreu's Law, which assumes a Abreu + (Demonstrators × Police) = (Arrests + Escapes) framework, omits the critical context of the demonstrations themselves. The proposed model adopts a different approach, focusing on identifying a subset of protesters who come into contact with the police and become incarcerated or evade capture, akin to the (Demonstrators × Police) = (Arrests + Escapes) framework. However, this leaves the group of protesters who remain largely unaffected by the encounter, which the model aims to incorporate to fully capture the dynamics of the 2019 Chilean protests.

A study comparing continuum spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting results with radio flux measurements in 166 K3 samples from the COSMOS and LOFAR-TCS surveys reveals discrepancies in derived star formation rates (SFRs). SED-based SFR estimates are generally lower, though the extent of the underestimation varies significantly. The discrepancy appears unrelated to mass or SFR errors associated with the measurements. Instead, the discrepancy is linked to the resolution of the radio data and the detection status of the 70 $\mu$m flux at specific wavelengths. Furthermore, the difference between SED and radio SFR estimates is explained by fitting single stellar population (SSP) models to galaxies spanning a broad range of ages, metallicities, and stellar populations. The results suggest that using SSP models overestimates the total stellar mass when galaxies contain diverse populations. Consequently, adopting this correction lowers the SED-based SFR estimates, reducing discrepancies with radio measurements. Lastly, the study finds that utilizing the [OIII] 5008 A line to estimate SFRs detects the same detection criteria as SED fitting but yields higher SFR estimates than both methods. The higher SFR estimates from [OIII] fitting are consistent with radio measurements, suggesting that [OIII] models may be more suitable for estimating stellar masses.

We identify a new class of polynomial expressions that lie within the boundary of the sum-of-squares cone, specifically those just outside the interior. This new category, called the positive strict boundary, encompasses the immediate passage from the sum-of-squares polynomials to polynomials with positive definite values. We demonstrate that binary forms and quartic forms belong to the positive strict boundary, and provide characterization methods for other cases, including ternary forms. These characterization methods are either new or fill gaps in existing proofs, and also reveal that certain previously known examples, such as the Dixon form, indeed have this property. Additionally, our work offers a distinct proof that the Dixon form is a boundary point within the SOS cone, and we establish that any homogenous polynomial with a strictly positive boundary must be non-degenerate.

The detection of neutrinos produced by non-standard processes, resulting in
leptonic non-unitarity, could be achieved using short baseline experiments and
neutrinos with short baselines like FASER$\nu$ in the LHC. Using simple
parametrizations for non-standard neutrino interactions, we examine the
conditions under which FASer$\nu$ may detect neutrinos produced via lepton
number violating or enhanced diphoton processes. We determine the minimum
possible values for the non-standard interaction parameters that could be
detected, considering the sensitivity of FASer$\nu$ to the number of observed
neutrinos and the mass distribution of heavy neutral leptons.
The work presents a symbolic resolution method for the Shannon expansion of regular expressions, maintaining the original format in the computed outcomes.

This research adapts the Profound-HR scene from Microsoft Research's database for video insertion, enabling high-resolution details to be captured. As a result, modified footage can accurately reflect fine-grained details within the original Profound-hr scenes. By leveraging external memory focus, our EMA network effectively combines scanning and processing to navigate these complex environments. By utilizing both external memory focus and the original network capabilities, we can improve navigation performance in the adapted Profound-HR dataset. Furthermore, the incorporation of attention modules leads to significant enhancements in mean absolute error and global localization success rates, achieving the best results to date.

We theoretically explore a new class of Weyl semimetals in two dimensions, known as square-root elevated-order Weyl semimetals, and develop a generalized Weyl-Hodge theory to support this finding. Our studies also highlight square-root elevated-order fermion triangles as a tangible example, while Hodge-fermion triangles exhibit mixed Chern-Schwinger charges and exhibit triangle cancellations in their variances.

This study examines the capability of the quasi-reversibility method in solving a problem that involves completing a set of equations for the time-dependent, source-free Maxwell's system. Available information in this case comprises one component of the electric field at two opposing time instances, allowing us to infer the missing field components and corresponding magnetic field components. Various mathematical techniques have been previously applied to address this problem, although many of these approaches come with significant computational requirements. In this instance, we aim to contribute to the resolution of this challenge by utilizing the quasi-reversibility method, a technique known for handling ill-posed problems effectively and maintaining stability in the face of inaccuracies in given data. Moreover, we provide a novel proof of convergence for the discrete solutions obtained through this method.

This paper introduces a vertex operator algebra structure for the parafermion current algebra associated with the Kac-Moody Lie superalgebra $K(osp(1|2n),k)$. We then establish the existence of a unique affine vertex algebra of the same type for any positive integer value of $n$ and any non-negative integer level $k$. Finally, we identify the algebra $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ as the sum of two subalgebras, specifically $W_p(\mathbb C^{2+4nk},p')$, where $p$ and $p'$ are distinct prime numbers derived from the Euler totient function of $2nk$.

The federated learning approach has been effectively applied in various domains, but one significant issue persists - a lack of effective methods to integrate pre-trained knowledge bases. Many existing models have already invested considerable time and resources in knowledge exploration, yet there are no unified strategies to combine these knowledge bases. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative proposal called Federated Discriminative Aggregation (FDA), a novel method to integrate pre-trained knowledge bases using the principles of federated learning. FDA treats each pre-trained model as a unique client and aims to create a unified model that can accurately differentiate between various classes through iterative communication and integrated learning, leveraging the core tenets of federated techniques. Experimental evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing notable performance improvements over baseline methods.

Approximately a decade back, the presence of grid cells in the rat's entorhinal cortex was first detected and confirmed through electrophysiological methods. Since then, computational models have been developed to explore the origins of grid cell functionality. This review provides a comprehensive summary of empirical findings related to grid cells and their location in the medial dorsal region of the entorhinal cortex. It also discusses the characteristics of grid cells and the various variables that influence grid cell behavior, including grid scale, distortion patterns, and stability. Furthermore, it examines existing models that attempt to replicate grid cell properties and highlights the need for model predictions to be validated experimentally. Given the significant implications grid cells may have for memory and navigation processes, there is a potential for their role in these cognitive functions to be investigated in greater detail.

Solar differential rotation significantly influences the generation of the Sun's global magnetic field through its tear-effect. A study using 3D solar-type models revealed a correlation between magnetic cycles and differential rotation in the Sun. This research suggests that magnetic cycles in stars could be influenced by differential rotation, and thus, this effect should be accounted for in the solar model. To further confirm this hypothesis, the project will analyze a range of rotating solar models with varying levels of differential rotation to better understand the relationship between a star's rotation and its magnetic cycles.

In quartic extensions of the rational numbers belonging to the Galois types $A_4$ and $S_4$, we investigate the growth patterns of elliptic curve rank. For $A_4$ quartic fields, this investigation is carried out using a collection of 226,800 such fields from the $\mathcal{Q} \leq 10^6$ range, during which we observe the prevalence of rank growth by examining the rank development matrices and their heatmaps. For $S_4$ quartic fields, we examine two large collections of 13,690,500 such fields in the $\mathcal{Q} \leq 10^6$ range, where $\mathcal{Q}$ is the limit of our computations. In doing so, we derive an estimated average rank difference of 0.336 for $A_4$ quartic fields and 0.338 for $S_4$ quartic fields. These estimated average rank differences, in combination with previously established theoretical lower bounds, offer a more precise approximation of the average rank of elliptic curves defined over $A_4$ and $S_4$ quartic fields.

This work investigates how quantum systems quantum thermodynamics as applied to systems modeled by quantum field theories dual to matter in AdS spaces, with a focus on event horizons and quantum fields that cause singularities or extreme pressure. Use of the duality allows examination of quantum systems at large, as well as small, scales. Use of simplified models provides an investigation of the limits of quantum systems expansion and the entanglement sudden death phenomenon.

This work delves into the concepts of discriminability duration and asymmetry velocity within a context of non-orthogonal quantum states evolving over time. Certain time scales characterizing these phenomena are identified and calculated for various models, such as a spin-1/2 system, providing an analysis of their connection to commonly used quantum velocity measures in the Bloch sphere. A research study is conducted to assess whether these time scales conform to specific inequality constraints, with a focus on understanding whether they adhere to the monotonicity principle as defined by asymmetry functions.

Consider the standard interval $I$ in the real number line and a set of $n$ points within it, denoted by $X_n$. For any given continuous function $f$ from $I$ to the real number line, the two-point operator $I_n$ is defined such that it approximates $f$ at the specified nodes $X_n$. This research aims to determine the maximum possible norm of $I_n$ across all configurations of $X_n$ in $I$, denoted as $M_n$. It is proven that for interval $I$, $M_n$ equals one when $n$ is odd, and slightly less than one when $n$ is even, specifically approximately $0.96586$. Furthermore, the research provides nearly optimal node arrangements to minimize the norm of $I_n$, and explores the case of polynomial interpolation of degree $n$.

Sub-terahertz and terahertz radiation has strong capabilities for non-destructive and non-functional imaging, making it an ideal tool for analyzing electronic systems. However, current near-field terahertz techniques struggle to capture dynamic electron behavior due to limited spatial resolution and weak radiation sources. This study presents an advanced terahertz imaging system that employs a high-performance hydrogen discharge lamp to create a bright near-field terahertz source. The achieved source brightness allows for high-resolution imaging, as demonstrated by a 10um spot size measurement. The thinfilm configuration of this lamp minimizes extraneous emission in the visible and ultraviolet spectrums, thus enabling high-contrast images. The near-field terahertz system's 10um resolution is also sufficient to identify sub-grid features, such as current density patterns in a micrometer-sized coplanar waveguide resonator, and effectively distinguishes between n-type and p-type doped silicon.

This lecture will introduce the concept of curved motivic spectra, a new extension of homotopy invariant sheaves with transfer that incorporates the idea of curvature. The motivation behind these objects stems from algebraic geometry's study of the K-theory of singular varieties using Chern classes. After providing a concise overview of the necessary foundations in motivic homotopy theory, the topic of interest will be explored in greater detail. The primary examples of curvature that can beskipped in this context are those arising from derived schemes, which will be examined from the perspective of condensed mathematics, the framework the speaker is primarily associated with. The primary objective of this examination of curved motivic homotopy theory is to establish the possibility of defining generalized Chern classes within the domain of algebraic geometry's projective geometry. The relevant questions in this area will be outlined in this examination. The primary sources of information that can be consulted for a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying concepts are the materials drawn from the lectures delivered in the summer school held in the Czech Republic in 2021, as well as the relevant research articles that can be found in the provided references.
